steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper that proposes a framework for evaluating the plausibility of context reliance in language models, applied to context-aware machine translation. Motivate the problem from interpretability, introduce the framework, and end with a list of contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Plausibility of rationales in NLP interpretability
- Why plausibility is hard to apply to generative language models
- Limits of current contrastive attribution studies
- Our framework: PECoRe
- Application to context-aware MT and what the paper does
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Plausibility of rationales in NLP interpretability
  - desiderata for rationales of model behavior; rationales = contributions of input tokens to predictions, computed with feature attribution
  - plausibility = alignment between model rationales and salient input words picked by human annotators
  - low-plausibility rationales go with generalization failures / biased predictions; useful to find models "right for the wrong reasons"
- Why it is hard for generative LMs
  - intuitive for classification with a single prediction, several challenges for generative LMs
  - large output space; semantically equivalent tokens compete for next-word prediction ("PC" vs "computer")
  - generations shaped by independent properties (semantic relatedness, topical coherence, grammatical correctness), hard to capture with one attribution score
  - autoregressive generation is iterative -> rationales for every generated token -> which generated tokens can have plausible contextual explanations?
- Limits of contrastive attribution studies
  - recent techniques use contrastive alternatives to disentangle aspects of predictions ("meowing" vs "screaming" for "The cat is ___": semantics, not grammaticality)
  - but they narrow evaluation to one generation step matching a phenomenon ("The pictures of the cat ___" -> "are", role of "pictures" in subject-verb agreement)
  - confined to small handcrafted benchmarks where tokens with plausible explanations are known in advance
  - may overlook context usage patterns that do not match linguistic intuitions
  - our position: identifying which generated tokens were most affected by context should be part of plausibility evaluation for generation
- PECoRe
  - Plausibility Evaluation of Context Reliance
  - end-to-end extraction of cue-target pairs: context-sensitive generated tokens + influential contextual cues (Figure 1)
  - uncovers context dependence in naturally occurring generations; quantifies plausibility where human annotations exist
  - compatible with contrastive attribution methods; no reference translations (distributional shifts); works on unannotated inputs
- Application to contextual MT
  - formalization in Section 3
  - bilingual and multilingual MT models
  - works with encoder-decoder and decoder-only LMs for any generation task; MT chosen for constrained output space + datasets with human rationales of context usage
  - tests on well-known discourse phenomena; benchmark context sensitivity metrics and attribution methods
  - unannotated examples: reasonable and questionable context reliance
- Contributions
  - PECoRe; quantitative plausibility evaluation beyond limited artificial settings
  - comparison of context sensitivity metrics and attribution methods on context-aware MT; limitations of current metrics
  - analysis of naturally-occurring translations; discourse-level phenomena; issues in context usage of context-aware MT models

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Research in NLP interpretability has defined different desiderata for rationales of model behaviors. By rationales we mean the contributions of the input tokens toward the predictions of the model, which are computed with feature attribution. One of these properties is plausibility. Plausibility is about how well the model rationales align with the salient input words that human annotators identify. Rationales with low plausibility usually go together with generalization failures or biased predictions, and they can be useful for finding cases where models are “right for the wrong reasons”. Plausibility is intuitive to interpret for classification tasks where there is a single prediction, but extending this methodology to generative language models (LMs) has several challenges. The first one is that LMs have a large output space, where tokens that are semantically equivalent (e.g. “ PC ” and “ computer ”) compete as candidates for next-word prediction. Another one is that LM generations come from optimization pressures that ensure independent properties like semantic relatedness, topical coherence and grammatical correctness, and a single attribution score can hardly capture all of these. Lastly, autoregressive generation is an iterative prediction process, so model rationales could be extracted for every generated token. This raises the issue of which of the generated tokens can have plausible contextual explanations.

Some recent attribution techniques for explaining language models use contrastive alternatives to disentangle different aspects of model predictions. For example, choosing “ meowing ” over “ screaming ” for “ The cat is ___ ” is motivated by semantic appropriateness, but not by grammaticality. But these studies get around the issues above by narrowing the evaluation down to a single generation step that matches a phenomenon of interest. For example, for the sentence “ The pictures of the cat ___ ”, a plausible rationale for predicting the word “ are ” should reflect the role of “ pictures ” in subject-verb agreement. This approach can be useful to validate model rationales, but it limits plausibility assessment to a small set of handcrafted benchmarks where we already know in advance which tokens have plausible explanations. It also risks missing important patterns of context usage, including the ones that do not immediately match linguistic intuitions. Because of this, we suggest that identifying which generated tokens were most affected by contextual input information should be an integral part of plausibility evaluation for language generation tasks.

- PECoRe (Plausibility Evaluation of Context Reliance)
  - end-to-end extraction of cue-target pairs from LM generations (Figure 1): context-sensitive generated tokens + their influential contextual cues
  - uncover context dependence in natural generations; quantify plausibility when human annotations exist
  - compatible with contrastive attribution; no reference translations (distributional shifts); works on unannotated inputs
- Application to contextual MT
  - formalized in Section 3; bilingual and multilingual MT models
  - usable with encoder-decoder and decoder-only LMs for any generation task, but MT chosen: constrained output space, datasets with human rationales
  - discourse phenomena; benchmark context sensitivity metrics and attribution methods for cue-target pairs
  - unannotated examples: reasonable and questionable context reliance
- Contributions
  - PECoRe framework; quantitative plausibility beyond limited artificial settings
  - comparison of metrics and attribution methods on context-aware MT, limits of current metrics
  - naturally-occurring translations: discourse-level phenomena, issues in context usage

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Research in NLP interpretability has defined different desiderata for rationales of model behaviors. By rationales we mean the contributions of the input tokens toward the predictions of the model, which are computed with feature attribution. One of these properties is plausibility. Plausibility is about how well the model rationales align with the salient input words that human annotators identify. Rationales with low plausibility usually go together with generalization failures or biased predictions, and they can be useful for finding cases where models are “right for the wrong reasons”. Plausibility is intuitive to interpret for classification tasks where there is a single prediction, but extending this methodology to generative language models (LMs) has several challenges. The first one is that LMs have a large output space, where tokens that are semantically equivalent (e.g. “ PC ” and “ computer ”) compete as candidates for next-word prediction. Another one is that LM generations come from optimization pressures that ensure independent properties like semantic relatedness, topical coherence and grammatical correctness, and a single attribution score can hardly capture all of these. Lastly, autoregressive generation is an iterative prediction process, so model rationales could be extracted for every generated token. This raises the issue of which of the generated tokens can have plausible contextual explanations.

Some recent attribution techniques for explaining language models use contrastive alternatives to disentangle different aspects of model predictions. For example, choosing “ meowing ” over “ screaming ” for “ The cat is ___ ” is motivated by semantic appropriateness, but not by grammaticality. But these studies get around the issues above by narrowing the evaluation down to a single generation step that matches a phenomenon of interest. For example, for the sentence “ The pictures of the cat ___ ”, a plausible rationale for predicting the word “ are ” should reflect the role of “ pictures ” in subject-verb agreement. This approach can be useful to validate model rationales, but it limits plausibility assessment to a small set of handcrafted benchmarks where we already know in advance which tokens have plausible explanations. It also risks missing important patterns of context usage, including the ones that do not immediately match linguistic intuitions. Because of this, we suggest that identifying which generated tokens were most affected by contextual input information should be an integral part of plausibility evaluation for language generation tasks.

To reach this goal, we propose a new interpretability framework that we call Plausibility Evaluation of Context Reliance (PECoRe). PECoRe allows the end-to-end extraction of cue-target token pairs from language model generations, as shown in Figure 1. These pairs are made of context-sensitive generated tokens and the contextual cues that influenced them. The pairs can uncover context dependence in generations that occur naturally, and when human annotations are available they help quantify how plausible the context usage of language models is. Our approach is compatible with modern attribution methods that use contrastive targets, it does not use reference translations so it stays clear of problematic distributional shifts, and it can be applied on unannotated inputs to identify context usage in model generations.

We formalize our approach in Section 3, and then we apply PECoRe to contextual machine translation (MT) to study how plausible context reliance is in bilingual and multilingual MT models. PECoRe can easily be used with encoder-decoder and decoder-only language models to interpret context usage in any text generation task, but we focus the evaluation on MT. This is because MT has a constrained output space that makes automatic assessment easier, and because there are MT datasets annotated with human rationales of context usage. We test PECoRe thoroughly on well-known discourse phenomena, and we benchmark several context sensitivity metrics and attribution methods for identifying cue-target pairs. At the end we apply PECoRe to unannotated examples and show some reasonable and some questionable cases of context reliance in the translations of MT models.

Our contributions are the following:

- We introduce PECoRe, an interpretability framework for detecting and attributing context reliance in language models. PECoRe makes it possible to evaluate plausibility quantitatively for language generation, beyond the limited artificial settings that previous literature explored.

- We compare how effective context sensitivity metrics and feature attribution methods are on the context-aware MT tasks, and show the limitations of the metrics that are currently in use.

- We apply PECoRe to translations that occur naturally to identify interesting discourse-level phenomena, and we discuss issues in the context usage abilities of context-aware MT models.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Research in NLP interpretability defines various desiderata for rationales of model behaviors, i.e. the contributions of input tokens toward model predictions computed with feature attribution [1]. One of these properties is plausibility, which corresponds to the alignment between model rationales and the salient input words identified by human annotators [2]. Low-plausibility rationales usually occur together with generalization failures or biased predictions and can be useful to identify cases of models being “right for the wrong reasons” [3]. However, while plausibility has an intuitive interpretation for classification tasks involving a single prediction, extending this methodology to generative language models (LMs) presents several challenges. First, LMs have a large output space where semantically equivalent tokens (e.g. “ PC ” and “ computer ”) are competing candidates for next-word prediction [4]. Moreover, LM generations are the product of optimization pressures to ensure independent properties such as semantic relatedness, topical coherence and grammatical correctness, which a single attribution score can hardly capture [5]. Finally, since autoregressive generation involves an iterative prediction process, model rationales could be extracted for every generated token. This raises the issue of which generated tokens can have plausible contextual explanations.

Recent attribution techniques for explaining language models incorporate contrastive alternatives to disentangle different aspects of model predictions (e.g. the choice of “ meowing ” over “ screaming ” for “ The cat is ___ ” is motivated by semantic appropriateness, but not by grammaticality) [6,7]. However, these studies avoid the issues above by narrowing the evaluation to a single generation step that matches a phenomenon of interest. For example, given the sentence “ The pictures of the cat ___ ”, a plausible rationale for the prediction of the word “ are ” should reflect the role of “ pictures ” in subject-verb agreement. While this approach can be useful to validate model rationales, it confines plausibility assessment to a small set of handcrafted benchmarks where the tokens with plausible explanations are known in advance. It also risks overlooking important patterns of context usage, including those that do not immediately match linguistic intuitions. In light of this, we suggest that identifying which generated tokens were most affected by contextual input information should be an integral part of plausibility evaluation for language generation tasks.

To achieve this goal, we propose a novel interpretability framework, which we call Plausibility Evaluation of Context Reliance (PECoRe). PECoRe enables the end-to-end extraction of cue-target token pairs, consisting of context-sensitive generated tokens and their respective influential contextual cues, from language model generations, as shown in Figure 1. These pairs can uncover context dependence in naturally occurring generations and, where human annotations are available, help quantify context usage plausibility in language models. Importantly, our approach is compatible with modern attribution methods using contrastive targets [5], avoids reference translations to stay clear of problematic distributional shifts [8], and can be applied on unannotated inputs to identify context usage in model generations.

After formalizing our approach in Section 3, we apply PECoRe to contextual machine translation (MT) to study the plausibility of context reliance in bilingual and multilingual MT models. While PECoRe can easily be used with encoder-decoder and decoder-only language models to interpret context usage in any text generation task, we focus our evaluation on MT, because its constrained output space facilitates automatic assessment and because MT datasets annotated with human rationales of context usage are available. We thoroughly test PECoRe on well-known discourse phenomena, benchmarking several context sensitivity metrics and attribution methods for identifying cue-target pairs. We conclude by applying PECoRe to unannotated examples and showing some reasonable and questionable cases of context reliance in MT model translations.

In sum, our contributions are the following:

- We introduce PECoRe, an interpretability framework to detect and attribute context reliance in language models. PECoRe enables a quantitative evaluation of plausibility for language generation beyond the limited artificial settings explored in previous literature.

- We compare the effectiveness of context sensitivity metrics and feature attribution methods on the context-aware MT tasks, showing the limitations of the metrics currently in use.

- We apply PECoRe to naturally-occurring translations to identify interesting discourse-level phenomena and discuss issues in the context usage abilities of context-aware MT models.
